title: Pave-GRPO: Beyond Instantaneous Guidance through Principled Average Velocity Decomposition

paper.title: Pave-GRPO: Beyond Instantaneous Guidance through Principled Average Velocity Decomposition
paper.abstract: Abstract. Post-training via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for aligning flow-based generative models with human preferences. However, the iterative denoising nature of flow models incurs substantial costs when generating group rollouts for policy-gradient updates, compelling existing methods to train with extremely few denoising steps. This temporal sparsity severely restricts preference optimization: reward feedback can only reach a handful of stages per trajectory, leaving the vast majority of intermediate denoising steps without direct supervision and thus compromising alignment granularity. To address this, we propose Pave-GRPO , which reformulates the GRPO objective through P rincipled a verage v elocity d e composition. Rather than generating expensive high-step rollouts, we maintain efficient few-step group sampling but decompose each coarse transition into an equivalent ensemble of finer sub-trajectories spanning multiple intermediate timesteps. This propagates reward feedback to a denser set of temporal stages for more comprehensive preference alignment without additional generation cost. This design offers two benefits: (i) zero-cost horizon expansion: through the direct reuse of piece-wise group samples and their associated rewards, Pave-GRPO significantly broadens the effective optimization scope under fixed sampling budgets; and (ii) comprehensive temporal supervision: by equivalently decomposing an instantaneous velocity target into a multi-timestep ensemble, it distributes reward signals across more intermediate stages of the denoising process, enabling finer-grained and more thorough preference optimization. Extensive experiments validate that Pave-GRPO effectively advances preference alignment across different reward settings, offering comprehensive performance enhancement.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in diffusion and flow models have enabled high-fidelity and flexible image synthesis across diverse domains. Correspondingly, the precise alignment of these generic pre-trained models with human preferences or task-specific constraints remains a non-trivial challenge. To this end, extensive research has explored post-training preference alignment techniques, which leverage feedback on model outputs to steer sampling trajectories toward desired endpoints. Such feedback can be derived from either direct human judgment ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) or automated ratings from reward models ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) , both reflecting specific preferences regarding the generated content. To leverage outcome feedback for optimization, a straightforward approach is pairwise comparison, which increases the likelihood ratio of preferred samples over non-preferred ones, termed Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Majumder et al., 2024 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . However, such comparisons only provide ranking information, making it difficult to distinguish between marginally and substantially better samples, thereby limiting optimization granularity. To address this, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025 ) samples a group of outputs from the same prompt and learns relative advantages through intra-group normalization. This eliminates shared baseline interference while reducing variance, thus improving both training stability and performance ceiling. Specifically for flow models, existing approaches ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Zhou et al., 2025b ) typically convert the deterministic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) sampling into Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) sampling to introduce the exploratory randomness required by GRPO. Nevertheless, due to the inherently multi-step iterative denoising process of flow models and GRPO’s reliance on large group sizes for accurate intra-group advantage estimation, generating a rollout group remains computationally expensive. This compels existing methods to adopt significantly fewer training steps compared to inference (for instance, 16 training steps versus the default 50 inference steps for FLUX.1 dev). Consequently, each trajectory provides only a handful of supervised transitions, leaving the vast majority of intermediate denoising stages without direct reward guidance. Such temporal sparsity severely constrains fine-grained preference alignment, as the optimization signal is compressed into sparse velocity updates at isolated timesteps, rather than propagating across the fine-grained denoising trajectory. In this work, we introduce Pave-GRPO to address this limitation. Rather than generating expensive high-step samples, we maintain efficient few-step group sampling but decompose each coarse transition into equivalently consecutive sub-fragments, backpropagating optimization signals to a denser set of temporal stages. This design stems from two observations. First, the iterative denoising process of a flow model is inherently a Markov process, in which each intermediate state serves as a sufficient statistic for the subsequent state, making these intermediate states reusable as shared targets for trajectory decomposition. Second, both pure SDE and hybrid ODE–SDE sampling yield tractable Gaussian probability paths. This allows the likelihood of few-step samples to be evaluated exactly under varying step configurations, enabling the recycling of advantages from cheap rollouts as supervision signals for multi-step optimization. The resulting decoupling yields two gains: (i) expanded effective optimization horizon without increased sampling cost, lifting the preference alignment ceiling; and (ii) comprehensive temporal supervision via shared intermediate regression targets, which distributes reward feedback across a denser set of temporal stages and enables finer-grained, more thorough preference optimization. Experiments across multiple settings confirm that Pave-GRPO consistently outperforms its competitors.

sections.heading: 2.1. Diffusion and flow models in visual generation
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) have become a dominant paradigm in generative modeling by learning to reverse an iterative noising process, enabling high-fidelity synthesis across diverse modalities including images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ; Labs, 2024 ) and video ( Guo et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wan et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025a ) . To mitigate the computational burden of operating in high-dimensional pixel spaces, Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ) perform the denoising process within a compressed latent representation. More recently, flow matching ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) emerges as a compelling alternative framework, which learns a continuous velocity field that transports probability mass from a noise distribution to the data distribution. This paradigm has proven highly effective, achieving state-of-the-art performance in high-quality image generation, as evidenced by models such as Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , FLUX series ( Labs, 2024 ; Labs, 2025 ) , and Qwen-Image ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , as well as in large-scale video synthesis with models including HunyuanVideo ( Team, 2025 ) , WAN series ( Wan et al., 2025 ) and LongCat-Video ( Team et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: 2.2. Preference alignment in flow models
sections.text: Aligning diffusion and flow models with human preferences has evolved from early PPO-based policy gradients ( Black et al., 2023 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) and DPO variants ( Peng et al., 2025 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ) toward more efficient online reinforcement learning frameworks, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . To adapt GRPO for flow matching, foundational works like Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) reformulate deterministic ODE sampling into equivalent SDE trajectories, facilitating stochastic exploration while preserving marginal distributions. Subsequent efforts have refined this paradigm from multiple perspectives. For instance, Flow-CPS ( Wang and Yu, 2025 ) addresses the noise inconsistency in SDE sampling to prevent residual artifacts, while MixGRPO ( Li et al., 2025a ) introduces a hybrid ODE-SDE strategy to enhance training efficiency. Further improvements include tree-structured rollouts in BranchGRPO ( Li et al., 2025b ) for gradient concentration, fine-grained credit assignment in TempFlow-GRPO ( He et al., 2025 ) and Granular-GRPO ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) , as well as dense multi-view reward mapping in MV-GRPO ( Bu et al., 2026 ) without costly sample regeneration. Despite these advances, existing approaches employ few-step denoising during training to reduce cost, yet require high-step inference for quality. Consequently, each training trajectory provides only a handful of supervised transitions, leaving the vast majority of intermediate denoising stages without direct reward guidance. This temporal sparsity intrinsically limits the granularity of preference alignment. To address this, our Pave-GRPO equivalently decomposes a low-step denoising trajectory into consecutive sub-fragments, decoupling the generation step budget from optimization granularity.

As depicted by the blue arrows in Fig. 2 , Flow models generate content through an iterative denoising process, which can be formalized as a trajectory of discrete states x t i x_{t_{i}} , indexed by time steps t i t_{i} spanning [1,0]. Since most reward models are trained exclusively on noise-free images ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , the reward score is usually computed at the endpoint of the denoising process x 0 x_{0} and is subsequently back-propagate to the intermediate point along the trajectory. Fundamentally, this iterative denoising process is a Markov Decision Process, which implies that: for any given intermediate state x t i + 1 x_{t_{i+1}} , all future decisions and states depend entirely on the current state, independent of the historical trajectory: (6) P ( x t i + 2 , … , x 0 ∣ x 1 , … , x t i + 1 ) = P ( x t i + 2 , … , x 0 ∣ x t i + 1 ) P(x_{t_{i+2}},\dots,x_{0}\mid x_{1},\dots,x_{t_{i+1}})=P(x_{t_{i+2}},\dots,x_{0}\mid x_{t_{i+1}}) As illustrated in Fig. 2 , for intermediate point x t i + 1 x_{t_{i+1}} on the denoising trajectory, its subsequent denoising trajectory is unaffected by its previous denoising trajectory. sections.heading: Gaussian structure.
sections.text: From the ODE/SDE formulations in Equations. 1 – 3 , the ODE governs a deterministic drift, while the SDE contributes a Gaussian diffusion. Therefore, both the pure trajectory (Eq. 7 ) and the hybrid trajectory (Eq. 8 ) yield Gaussian-distributed states, albeit with different means and variances.

sections.heading: Marginal and SNR equivalence.
sections.text: For marginal-preserving SDE in Eq. 2 , it share the same Fokker–Planck equation ( Øksendal, 2003 ) with its paired probability-flow ODE, so they follow the identical density-evolution law. Consequently, any two trajectories that start from the same marginal at t i t_{i} and end at the same timestep t i + 1 t_{i+1} will exhibit the same marginal distribution. Meanwhile, for SNR-preserving SDE in Eq. 3 , the signal-to-noise ratio is dictated solely by the diffusion coefficients at the target time ( Wang and Yu, 2025 ) , independent of the denoising path. Thus, pure and hybrid sampling yield exactly the same marginal/SNR at t i + 1 t_{i+1} . As shown in Equations 1 – 3 , each ODE/SDE operator contains exactly one velocity v θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) predicted by model, indicating that the optimization of a single operator at specific time is intrinsically the optimization of the model’s velocity field at the same time. sections.heading: Pipeline Overview
sections.text: As illustrated in Fig. 3 , Pave-GRPO operates through three tightly coupled stages: (i) Efficient Group Rollouts. For each prompt, we generate a group of G G trajectories via lightweight few-step pure-SDE sampling. This preserves the exploratory stochasticity required by GRPO while keeping the generation budget minimal. (ii) Relative Advantage Estimation. A reward model evaluates the terminal noise-free output of each trajectory, yielding scores { r g } g = 1 G \{r_{g}\}_{g=1}^{G} . These are normalized within the group to produce relative advantages { A ^ g } g = 1 G \{\hat{A}^{g}\}_{g=1}^{G} . (iii) Principled Velocity Decomposition. Each coarse transition 𝐱 t i → 𝐱 t i + 1 \mathbf{x}_{t_{i}}\!\to\!\mathbf{x}_{t_{i+1}} from the pure-SDE rollout is treated as a fixed boundary condition for constructing equivalent hybrid ODE–SDE sub-trajectories with varying step granularities K ∈ 𝒮 K\!\in\!\mathcal{S} (e.g., K = 2 , 3 K\!=\!2,3 ). Leveraging the Markov property and the tractable Gaussian probability paths shared by ODE and SDE operators, we evaluate the exact likelihood of the observed state 𝐱 t i + 1 \mathbf{x}_{t_{i+1}} under these finer hybrid distributions without generating additional samples . The policy is then optimized to increase the probability of high-advantage transitions across all decomposed paths, effectively splitting the single coarse velocity target into K K piecewise sub-velocities. This propagates reward feedback to intermediate timesteps that would otherwise remain unsupervised, achieving denser temporal supervision at zero extra sampling cost.

sections.heading: 5.1. Implementation Details
sections.text: Training and evaluation data . Following prior works ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025b ) , we adopt the HPD ( Wu et al., 2023 ) dataset for both training and evaluation, which contains over 100K diverse prompts, with a held-out set of 400 prompts reserved for testing. Additionally, we evaluate on UniGenBench ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , a unified benchmark comprising 600 meticulously designed prompts, providing fine-grained evaluations across 10 different dimensions. Backbone and baselines . All experiments are conducted on Flux.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) , a widely adopted text-to-image backbone comprising 12B parameters. We compare against both conventional and recent methods, including Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , and Flow-CPS ( Wang and Yu, 2025 ) . Evaluation metrics . For a comprehensive assessment of generation quality, we evaluate across three types of metrics: (i) CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) for image-text alignment; (ii) dedicated reward models: ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , HPS-v2/v3 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , UnifiedReward-v1/v2 ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and Pick-Score ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) ; and (iii) fine-grained semantic evaluation on UniGenBench ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . It leverages an MLLM-based assessor to score 10 primary dimensions (including attribute binding, spatial layout, world knowledge, text rendering, etc.), providing a holistic evaluation on conceptual fidelity, visual appeal, and overall text-image alignment. Training settings . We perform full-parameter training with a batch size of 8, using the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} . To enhance computational efficiency, we employ bfloat16 mixed precision for training acceleration. Our Pave-GRPO builds upon the variant of FlowGRPO ( He et al., 2025 ) , which adopts step-wise reward assessment to ensure reliable credit assignment and faster convergence, using a fixed group size of 12 for sample generation. All baselines adopt the same acceleration strategy for fair comparison. Following prior work ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , we train the model with 16 denoising steps, with pure-SDE sampling conducted at timesteps { 0 , 2 , 4 , 6 } \{0,2,4,6\} , while evaluation switches to 50 steps for higher generation quality. sections.heading: 5.2. Qualitative Results
sections.text: The visual comparison of different methods is provided in Figure. 4 . It is observed that Pave-GRPO consistently outperforms its competitors in semantic alignment, visual fidelity, and aesthetic appeal across both reward model settings. In the “anime schoolgirls” and “daffodil” cases (HPS-v2), Pave-GRPO renders fine facial features and intricate textures with superior clarity and vibrant color harmony, whereas baseline Flux.1-dev produces relatively dim and less expressive results. For the “tropical fish knight” example, Pave-GRPO enhances the character’s material realism by vividly synthesizing metallic reflections, fabric folds, and ambient lighting that are largely absent in Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO. Similarly, in the “barbarian” and “fruit basket” examples (HPS-v3), Pave-GRPO enriches the compositions with elaborate contextual details—such as architectural elements in the background, diverse fruit varieties, and nuanced surface materials—significantly elevating the immersive quality and photorealistic atmosphere of the generated images. Finally, in the “train” case, Pave-GRPO not only generates a structurally coherent locomotive but also optimizes the environmental lighting and atmospheric depth to create a more compelling and expansive scene composition. These results validate that Pave-GRPO effectively harnesses the reward signal to improve both subject fidelity and scene complexity without sacrificing overall visual harmony.

sections.heading: 5.3. Subjective Evaluation
sections.text: Tab. 1 compares the proposed method under four reward settings on both in-domain and out-of-domain metrics. Pave-GRPO consistently outperforms competitors across all configurations, validating its robustness for preference alignment. It achieves strong results under both marginal-distribution-preserving and SNR-preserving SDE frameworks, as our fine-grained decomposition is agnostic to specific path constructions. Crucially, out-of-domain gains confirm these improvements reflect intrinsic generalization rather than reward overfitting. For the evaluation on UniGenBench ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , the proposed Pave-GRPO( ℱ sde mar \mathcal{F}_{\text{sde}}^{\text{mar}} ) attains the highest overall score ( 63.96 ), establishing new state-of-the-art results. It significantly surpasses the Flux.1-dev baseline in Knowledge, Attribute, Action, and Text, and exceeds Flow-GRPO by +1.31 overall (+2.03 Attribute, +4.31 Text). These gains demonstrate that the fine-grained optimization enhances complex semantic understanding and compositional generation beyond superficial aesthetic metrics.

sections.heading: 5.4. Analysis and Ablations
sections.text: Effect of multi-path optimization. Given that Pave-GRPO is built upon Flow-GRPO that also employs marginal-preserving SDE ( ℱ sde mar \mathcal{F}_{\text{sde}}^{\text{mar}} ), the comparison between Flow-GRPO and Pave-GRPO ( ℱ sde mar \mathcal{F}_{\text{sde}}^{\text{mar}} ) in Table 1 and Table 2 constitutes a direct ablation, in which the consistent superiority of Pave-GRPO across different dimensions validates its efficacy in advancing text-to-image preference alignment. The corresponding reward curves during training are also provided in Figure 5 , corroborating its stable performance improvement. Sensitivity to decomposition factors. Since our method introduces a decomposition-factor set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} that determines the sub-step granularity in the hybrid paths, we further assess its robustness by systematically varying 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . Results in Table. 3 shows that the proposed methods consistently outperform the baseline under different 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , confirming the effectiveness of multi-path decomposition across various sub-step configurations. However, it is also observed that increasing | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| proportionally expands the number of hybrid paths, thereby raising computational overhead per-training step. Meanwhile, performance improvements exhibit diminishing returns and do not scale monotonically with larger 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , indicating that excessively fine-grained decomposition yields only marginal gains at the cost of increased training cost. Therefore, unless otherwise specified, we adopt 𝒮 = { 2 , 3 } \mathcal{S}=\{2,3\} for all comparative experiments in this paper, achieving a favorable balance between performance and computational efficiency.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we present Pave-GRPO, a novel framework that enhances GRPO post-training for preference alignment of flow models. Instead of expensive high-step rollouts, it keeps lightweight, few-step pure-SDE sampling and breaks each coarse trajectory into consecutive smaller segments. Based on the Markov property of iterative denoising and the tractable Gaussian probability paths shared by ODE and SDE forms, it reuses cheap rollout advantages as dense supervision signals for multi-step optimization. This separates the generation step budget from the optimization granularity, extending the effective optimization range while implicitly enforcing piecewise velocity consistency through shared intermediate targets. As a result, the model achieves more comprehensive preference alignment and stronger cross-metric generalization with no extra sampling cost. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev confirm that our carefully designed trajectory decomposition outperforms its competitors across different reward settings.

Post-training via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for aligning flow-based generative models with human preferences. However, the iterative denoising nature of flow models incurs substantial costs when generating group rollouts for policy-gradient updates, compelling existing methods to train with extremely few denoising steps. This temporal sparsity severely restricts preference optimization: reward feedback can only reach a handful of stages per trajectory, leaving the vast majority of intermediate denoising steps without direct supervision and thus compromising alignment granularity. To address this, we propose Pave-GRPO , which reformulates the GRPO objective through P rincipled a verage v elocity d e composition. Rather than generating expensive high-step rollouts, we maintain efficient few-step group sampling but decompose each coarse transition into an equivalent ensemble of finer sub-trajectories spanning multiple intermediate timesteps. This propagates reward feedback to a denser set of temporal stages for more comprehensive preference alignment without additional generation cost. This design offers two benefits: (i) zero-cost horizon expansion: through the direct reuse of piece-wise group samples and their associated rewards, Pave-GRPO significantly broadens the effective optimization scope under fixed sampling budgets; and (ii) comprehensive temporal supervision: by equivalently decomposing an instantaneous velocity target into a multi-timestep ensemble, it distributes reward signals across more intermediate stages of the denoising process, enabling finer-grained and more thorough preference optimization. Extensive experiments validate that Pave-GRPO effectively advances preference alignment across different reward settings, offering comprehensive performance enhancement. 1. Introduction Recent advances in diffusion and flow models have enabled high-fidelity and flexible image synthesis across diverse domains. Correspondingly, the precise alignment of these generic pre-trained models with human preferences or task-specific constraints remains a non-trivial challenge. To this end, extensive research has explored post-training preference alignment techniques, which leverage feedback on model outputs to steer sampling trajectories toward desired endpoints. Such feedback can be derived from either direct human judgment ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) or automated ratings from reward models ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) , both reflecting specific preferences regarding the generated content. To leverage outcome feedback for optimization, a straightforward approach is pairwise comparison, which increases the likelihood ratio of preferred samples over non-preferred ones, termed Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ( Majumder et al., 2024 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . However, such comparisons only provide ranking information, making it difficult to distinguish between marginally and substantially better samples, thereby limiting optimization granularity. To address this, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025 ) samples a group of outputs from the same prompt and learns relative advantages through intra-group normalization. This eliminates shared baseline interference while reducing variance, thus improving both training stability and performance ceiling. Specifically for flow models, existing approaches ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Zhou et al., 2025b ) typically convert the deterministic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) sampling into Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) sampling to introduce the exploratory randomness required by GRPO. Nevertheless, due to the inherently multi-step iterative denoising process of flow models and GRPO’s reliance on large group sizes for accurate intra-group advantage estimation, generating a rollout group remains computationally expensive. This compels existing methods to adopt significantly fewer training steps compared to inference (for instance, 16 training steps versus the default 50 inference steps for FLUX.1 dev). Consequently, each trajectory provides only a handful of supervised transitions, leaving the vast majority of intermediate denoising stages without direct reward guidance. Such temporal sparsity severely constrains fine-grained preference alignment, as the optimization signal is compressed into sparse velocity updates at isolated timesteps, rather than propagating across the fine-grained denoising trajectory. In this work, we introduce Pave-GRPO to address this limitation. Rather than generating expensive high-step samples, we maintain efficient few-step group sampling but decompose each coarse transition into equivalently consecutive sub-fragments, backpropagating optimization signals to a denser set of temporal stages. This design stems from two observations. First, the iterative denoising process of a flow model is inherently a Markov process, in which each intermediate state serves as a sufficient statistic for the subsequent state, making these intermediate states reusable as shared targets for trajectory decomposition. Second, both pure SDE and hybrid ODE–SDE sampling yield tractable Gaussian probability paths. This allows the likelihood of few-step samples to be evaluated exactly under varying step configurations, enabling the recycling of advantages from cheap rollouts as supervision signals for multi-step optimization. The resulting decoupling yields two gains: (i) expanded effective optimization horizon without increased sampling cost, lifting the preference alignment ceiling; and (ii) comprehensive temporal supervision via shared intermediate regression targets, which distributes reward feedback across a denser set of temporal stages and enables finer-grained, more thorough preference optimization. Experiments across multiple settings confirm that Pave-GRPO consistently outperforms its competitors. 2. Related work 2.1. Diffusion and flow models in visual generation Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) have become a dominant paradigm in generative modeling by learning to reverse an iterative noising process, enabling high-fidelity synthesis across diverse modalities including images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ; Labs, 2024 ) and video ( Guo et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wan et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025a ) . To mitigate the computational burden of operating in high-dimensional pixel spaces, Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ) perform the denoising process within a compressed latent representation. More recently, flow matching ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) emerges as a compelling alternative framework, which learns a continuous velocity field that transports probability mass from a noise distribution to the data distribution. This paradigm has proven highly effective, achieving state-of-the-art performance in high-quality image generation, as evidenced by models such as Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , FLUX series ( Labs, 2024 ; Labs, 2025 ) , and Qwen-Image ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , as well as in large-scale video synthesis with models including HunyuanVideo ( Team, 2025 ) , WAN series ( Wan et al., 2025 ) and LongCat-Video ( Team et al., 2025 ) . 2.2. Preference alignment in flow models Aligning diffusion and flow models with human preferences has evolved from early PPO-based policy gradients ( Black et al., 2023 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) and DPO variants ( Peng et al., 2025 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ) toward more efficient online reinforcement learning frameworks, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . To adapt GRPO for flow matching, foundational works like Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) reformulate deterministic ODE sampling into equivalent SDE trajectories, facilitating stochastic exploration while preserving marginal distributions. Subsequent efforts have refined this paradigm from multiple perspectives. For instance, Flow-CPS ( Wang and Yu, 2025 ) addresses the noise inconsistency in SDE sampling to prevent residual artifacts, while MixGRPO ( Li et al., 2025a ) introduces a hybrid ODE-SDE strategy to enhance training efficiency. Further improvements include tree-structured rollouts in BranchGRPO ( Li et al., 2025b ) for gradient concentration, fine-grained credit assignment in TempFlow-GRPO ( He et al., 2025 ) and Granular-GRPO ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) , as well as dense multi-view reward mapping in MV-GRPO ( Bu et al., 2026 ) without costly sample regeneration. Despite these advances, existing approaches employ few-step denoising during training to reduce cost, yet require high-step inference for quality. Consequently, each training trajectory provides only a handful of supervised transitions, leaving the vast majority of intermediate denoising stages without direct reward guidance. This temporal sparsity intrinsically limits the granularity of preference alignment. To address this, our Pave-GRPO equivalently decomposes a low-step denoising trajectory into consecutive sub-fragments, decoupling the generation step budget from optimization granularity. 3. Experiments 5.1. Implementation Details Training and evaluation data . Following prior works ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025b ) , we adopt the HPD ( Wu et al., 2023 ) dataset for both training and evaluation, which contains over 100K diverse prompts, with a held-out set of 400 prompts reserved for testing. Additionally, we evaluate on UniGenBench ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , a unified benchmark comprising 600 meticulously designed prompts, providing fine-grained evaluations across 10 different dimensions. Backbone and baselines . All experiments are conducted on Flux.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) , a widely adopted text-to-image backbone comprising 12B parameters. We compare against both conventional and recent methods, including Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , and Flow-CPS ( Wang and Yu, 2025 ) . Evaluation metrics . For a comprehensive assessment of generation quality, we evaluate across three types of metrics: (i) CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) for image-text alignment; (ii) dedicated reward models: ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , HPS-v2/v3 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , UnifiedReward-v1/v2 ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and Pick-Score ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) ; and (iii) fine-grained semantic evaluation on UniGenBench ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . It leverages an MLLM-based assessor to score 10 primary dimensions (including attribute binding, spatial layout, world knowledge, text rendering, etc.), providing a holistic evaluation on conceptual fidelity, visual appeal, and overall text-image alignment. It is observed that Pave-GRPO consistently outperforms its competitors in semantic alignment, visual fidelity, and aesthetic appeal across both reward model settings. In the “anime schoolgirls” and “daffodil” cases (HPS-v2), Pave-GRPO renders fine facial features and intricate textures with superior clarity and vibrant color harmony, whereas baseline Flux.1-dev produces relatively dim and less expressive results. For the “tropical fish knight” example, Pave-GRPO enhances the character’s material realism by vividly synthesizing metallic reflections, fabric folds, and ambient lighting that are largely absent in Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO. Similarly, in the “barbarian” and “fruit basket” examples (HPS-v3), Pave-GRPO enriches the compositions with elaborate contextual details—such as architectural elements in the background, diverse fruit varieties, and nuanced surface materials—significantly elevating the immersive quality and photorealistic atmosphere of the generated images. Since our method introduces a decomposition-factor set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} that determines the sub-step granularity in the hybrid paths, we further assess its robustness by systematically varying 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . Conclusion In this work, we present Pave-GRPO, a novel framework that enhances GRPO post-training for preference alignment of flow models. Instead of expensive high-step rollouts, it keeps lightweight, few-step pure-SDE sampling and breaks each coarse trajectory into consecutive smaller segments. Based on the Markov property of iterative denoising and the tractable Gaussian probability paths shared by ODE and SDE forms, it reuses cheap rollout advantages as dense supervision signals for multi-step optimization. This separates the generation step budget from the optimization granularity, extending the effective optimization range while implicitly enforcing piecewise velocity consistency through shared intermediate targets. As a result, the model achieves more comprehensive preference alignment and stronger cross-metric generalization with no extra sampling cost. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev confirm that our carefully designed trajectory decomposition outperforms its competitors across different reward settings. References Black et al. (2023) K. Black, M.
